variants.content: Define one exception type for invalid input to the record fetchers, because mixed None, error-dict and ValueError returns were leaking into caches. Plan: (1) Add class RecordInputError(ValueError) at module level in app/svc_{seed}_core.py. (2) Single-record functions (fetch_record_{seed}_N and similar) raise it for any id below 1, before doing any work. (3) Never return None or an error dict to signal bad input. (4) Batch functions don't raise; they follow the partial-result contract. (5) The offending id may appear in the exception message but never in logs; the logging rule still applies. (6) Tests cover id 0 and a negative id. Alternatives: returning Optional (rejected: ambiguous with not-found) and a Result type (rejected: unidiomatic in this codebase). (7) Rollout - the first fetcher to validate its input introduces the class; the rest adopt it as they are touched, rather than in one sweeping change, to keep diffs reviewable. (8) Callers that currently check for None after a fetch keep working until their fetcher is migrated, then switch to catching RecordInputError.

variants.title: Never log record ids or function arguments
variants.content: Never log record ids or function arguments from the record service, because compliance treats request data as customer data; log counts and durations instead.

variants.title: Never log record ids or function arguments
variants.content: Never log record ids or function arguments in app/svc_{seed}_core.py, because compliance classifies request data as customer data and the log pipeline isn't approved for it (audit finding, June 2026). That includes debug logs and messages passed to logger.exception; log counts and durations instead. If an error needs an id to be debuggable, put it in the exception for the caller to handle, not in a log line. The audit sampled two weeks of logs and found ids in debug output from three modules; this one was cleaned up first. Applies to print() as well, since stdout is shipped to the same pipeline.

variants.title: Keep request data out of the record service's logs
variants.content: Keep request data out of the record service's logs, because the June 2026 audit classified record ids as customer data. Plan: (1) Never log record ids, function arguments or returned records, at any level, including debug. (2) Log what operators need without request data: that a call happened, counts and durations. (3) Exceptions may carry an id for the caller, but logger.exception messages must not include it. (4) print() follows the same rule, since stdout ships to the same pipeline. (5) Use the module logger, logging.getLogger(__name__), so levels can be set per module.

seed_decisions.title: Return a tombstone for deleted records
seed_decisions.content: Return a tombstone, {'id': record_id, 'deleted': True}, for deleted records instead of raising, because the export job counts tombstones to reconcile deletions.

seed_decisions.title: Name hand-written functions verb_noun without the slot suffix
seed_decisions.content: Name new hand-written public functions verb_noun (for example build_report or list_slots) and keep the service-number suffix only on the generated per-slot fetchers, because the slot registry parses the generated names and hand-written names must not collide with that pattern.

seed_decisions.title: Prefix versions with v
seed_decisions.content: Prefix version strings with a lowercase v, as in v1.4.0, so they match the git tags exactly.

variants.title: Bound every cache at 256 entries
variants.content: Use functools.lru_cache(maxsize=256) for any memoisation in the record service, never an unbounded cache, because the worker runs on a fixed memory budget.

variants.title: Cap caches with lru_cache(maxsize=256) after the OOM incident
variants.content: Cap caches in app/svc_{seed}_core.py with functools.lru_cache(maxsize=256), because an unbounded cache took the worker down. In August a dict-based cache was added around the record fetchers to speed up the dashboard; it never evicted, grew to several hundred MB over a week, and the container was OOM-killed (#63). functools.cache and lru_cache(maxsize=None) have the same problem, so both were ruled out in review. 256 entries covered the dashboard's hot set, judging by the access logs at the time. If a function needs caching, wrap it with lru_cache(maxsize=256) directly so cache_info() stays available to the metrics endpoint. A per-call dict passed in by the caller is fine for request-scoped reuse; the rule is about anything that outlives a call. Raised again in review of #67, where a contributor reached for functools.cache because it is shorter; the reviewer pointed back here.

variants.title: Introduce bounded memoisation for record reads
variants.content: Introduce bounded memoisation for record reads, because repeated reads of the same ids dominate dashboard latency. Plan: (1) Mechanism - functools.lru_cache from the standard library; no third-party cache and no hand-rolled dict, since eviction is the part that is easy to get wrong. (2) Size - maxsize=256 for every cache in app/svc_{seed}_core.py; an unbounded size (maxsize=None, functools.cache) is not allowed. (3) Observability - keep the cache object reachable at module level so cache_info() can be scraped; don't hide it inside a closure. (4) Invalidation - records are immutable for a given id, so no TTL is needed now; revisit if records become writable. (5) Rollout - start with the hottest fetchers, measure, then extend. Alternatives considered: a Redis cache (rejected: new infrastructure for a single process) and cachetools.TTLCache (rejected: a new dependency for no current need). Risks noted at sign-off: memoising a function that returns a mutable dict lets one caller's mutation leak to the next, so callers must treat cached records as read-only; and a cache on a function that raises caches nothing, which is the behaviour we want for invalid ids. The 256 figure is per cache, not shared across the module.

variants.title: Fail fast in fetchers; let the client retry
variants.content: Fetchers make one upstream attempt and fail fast on a timeout; never add retry loops inside them, because the client already retries and nested retries caused the #55 request storm.

variants.title: Keep retries out of fetchers after the #55 request storm
variants.content: Don't put retry loops inside the fetch functions in app/svc_{seed}_core.py; retries belong to the client layer, because nested retries in #55 turned one slow dependency into a nine-fold request storm. During that incident the client retried three times, the gateway retried three times, and a fetcher wrapped its own call in a three-attempt loop, so one slow upstream received nine requests per user action and fell over completely. The post-incident review assigned retry ownership to the client, which also owns the backoff policy. A fetcher makes at most one upstream call; on a timeout it fails fast with a typed error the client's retry policy can recognise.

variants.title: Make record fetchers fail fast instead of retrying
variants.content: Make record fetchers fail fast instead of retrying, because the client owns retries and backoff. Plan from the #55 post-incident review: (1) One attempt - each fetcher in app/svc_{seed}_core.py calls the upstream at most once per invocation. (2) No loops - no retry, backoff or sleep inside fetchers, including a single extra attempt. (3) Typed failure - on a timeout, raise a module-level error the client can match, instead of returning None or a placeholder record. (4) Ownership - retry count and backoff live in the client's policy, so they can be tuned in one place. (5) Considered: a small in-fetcher retry with jitter (rejected: it multiplies with client and gateway retries, which is exactly what caused the storm).

seed_decisions.title: Manage dependencies and commands with uv
seed_decisions.content: Use uv for every dependency and script command in this repo (uv sync, uv run pytest), never pip or a bare python, because uv.lock is the source of truth and pip installs drift from it. CI runs uv sync --frozen and fails if the lock is stale.

seed_decisions.title: Return the plain string OK from health()
seed_decisions.content: The load balancer expects the literal body OK from the health check; return the plain string 'OK' and nothing else.

variants.title: Keep fetchers as plain module functions
variants.content: Expose record lookups as module-level functions (or a dict of them), never a repository, service or manager class, because #77's RecordRepository duplicated every function. Exception classes are fine.

variants.title: Don't wrap the fetchers in a class layer
variants.content: Keep app/svc_{seed}_core.py a module of plain functions and don't add a repository, service or manager class over the fetchers, because the RecordRepository introduced in #77 duplicated every fetcher as a method and was removed two months later. Every caller then had to construct an object it did not need, and the class and the functions drifted apart. Callers import functions directly; a dispatch table (a dict from slot to function) is fine when a lookup by slot is needed. Exception classes and plain data are not affected by this rule.

variants.title: Adopt a no-class-layer rule for the record service
variants.content: Adopt a no-class-layer rule for the record service, because an interface with one implementation added code without adding behaviour. Plan: (1) Public API - module-level functions only. (2) Lookups - a function, or a dict mapping keys to functions, never an object with methods. (3) Not allowed - repository, service, manager or client classes wrapping the fetchers, including singletons. (4) Allowed - exception classes. (5) Revisit only if a second storage backend actually exists.

variants.title: Write files atomically with mode 0o600
variants.content: Write every file the record service produces to a temp file in the same directory and os.replace it into place with mode 0o600, because a crash mid-write left a truncated export the importer accepted.

variants.title: Replace output files atomically after the truncated export
variants.content: Replace output files atomically in app/svc_{seed}_core.py: write to a temporary file in the destination's directory, then os.replace it over the target, because a worker killed mid-write in #84 left a half-written export that the importer accepted as complete. Writing in place meant readers could see a partial file at any moment, and a crash left it that way. The temp file must live in the same directory so os.replace stays an atomic rename on one filesystem. Exports hold customer records, so the final file has mode 0o600, readable only by the service user; the default umask produced world-readable files.

variants.title: Adopt atomic, private writes for service output files
variants.content: Adopt atomic, private writes for every file the record service writes, because partial and world-readable exports both caused incidents. Plan: (1) Temp file - create it in the target's directory (tempfile.mkstemp with dir=), so the final rename stays on one filesystem. (2) Write and flush the full content to the temp file. (3) Replace - os.replace(temp, target); never write the target in place. (4) Permissions - the result is mode 0o600. (5) Cleanup - remove the temp file if writing fails, so no stray files are left. (6) Considered: writing in place with fsync (rejected: readers can still see a partial file).

seed_decisions.title: Treat calls over 150 ms as slow
seed_decisions.content: Treat an upstream call that takes more than 150 ms as slow, because the #99 latency review tightened the earlier 200 ms threshold.

history.title: Treat calls over 200 ms as slow
history.content: Treat an upstream call that takes more than 200 ms as slow, because that matched the gateway's alerting at the time.

variants.title: Read configuration at call time, never at import
variants.content: Read settings from os.environ inside the function that needs them, never at import time, because the test runner and the worker set variables after import.

variants.title: Never read configuration at import time
variants.content: Never read configuration at import time in the service modules; read os.environ inside the function that needs it, because the test runner and the worker set environment variables after import and import-time reads froze stale values (this bit us twice with the region setting). Secrets never go in code or in default values. Tests that need a setting use monkeypatch.setenv inside the test, which only works because nothing reads the variable at import. Defaults for non-secret settings live next to the read, as the second argument to os.environ.get.

variants.title: Read configuration at call time in every service module
variants.content: Read configuration at call time in every service module, because import-time reads froze stale values twice. Plan from the region-setting incidents: (1) Where - os.environ is read inside the function that uses the value, on every call. (2) Defaults - a non-secret default sits next to the read as the second argument to os.environ.get; secrets have no default. (3) Not allowed - module-level constants computed from the environment, and caching a setting at import. (4) Tests - set variables with monkeypatch.setenv inside the test, which only works because nothing reads them at import. (5) Considered: a settings object loaded once at startup (rejected: it brings back the stale-value problem for the worker).

seed_decisions.title: Publish bare semantic versions
seed_decisions.content: Publish versions as bare semantic versions such as 1.4.0; the package index rejects a leading letter.

seed_decisions.title: Test every new public function before finishing
seed_decisions.content: Every new public function in app/ needs at least one test before the change is finished, and run uv run pytest tests/ -q before reporting done, because CI blocks merges on missing tests for new symbols.

variants.title: Never write back after a forgiving read
variants.content: Use a forgiving reader (one that turns a corrupt file into []) only for display; a function that writes the file back must load it with a reader that raises on corruption, because a forgiving read before a write wiped a queued export.

variants.title: Load strictly before writing after the wiped export
variants.content: Load files strictly in any function that writes them back, because a forgiving read before a write replaced a queued export with an empty list in #86. load_records in app/svc_{seed}_core.py deliberately reads a corrupt or unreadable file as empty, which is right for the dashboard: showing nothing beats crashing. But an append built on it read the damaged file as [], added one record and saved, silently discarding everything that was there. Display paths keep the forgiving reader; write paths parse with json.load and let the decode error propagate, so a human can recover the file. A missing file may still be treated as empty.

variants.title: Separate forgiving reads from strict reads before writes
variants.content: Separate forgiving reads from strict reads, because a corrupt file read as empty before a write erased queued data. Plan: (1) Display paths may use a reader that returns [] for a corrupt or unreadable file. (2) Any function that writes a file back loads it with a strict parser and lets a decode error propagate; it never writes after a failed parse. (3) A missing file may be treated as empty on both paths. (4) Tests cover a corrupt file on every write path and assert the file is untouched. (5) Considered: backing up the file before every write (rejected: it hides the corruption instead of surfacing it).

seed_decisions.title: Keep the record dict shape stable for per-slot fetchers
seed_decisions.content: Keep the record dict shape {'id': ..., 'slot': ...} stable for every fetch_record_{seed}_N function, because the export job and two dashboards index into it by key and break on extra or renamed fields. In #49 someone added a 'source' field to three fetchers, and the export job's strict schema check rejected every row for a day before anyone noticed. If a caller needs more data, add a separate function that returns a new shape rather than widening the record. Slot numbers are positional and stable: fetch_record_{seed}_7 always returns slot 7, so never renumber functions when one is removed; leave a gap instead. The export job's schema lives in another repository and is versioned separately, so even an additive field needs a coordinated release there first; that coordination cost is why new data goes into new functions. The incident write-up is linked from #49; the follow-up added a schema-contract test on the export side, not here.

variants.title: Use the standard library before any third-party package
variants.content: Use the standard library before any third-party package, and don't add a dependency to pyproject.toml without asking, because each new package needs a licence and security review.

variants.title: Ask before adding third-party dependencies
variants.content: Do not add third-party dependencies to the record service without asking first; prefer the standard library (functools, json, time, datetime), because every new package needs a licence and security review that takes weeks.

variants.title: Keep the record service on the standard library unless a dependency is approved
variants.content: Keep the record service on the standard library unless a dependency is approved, because every new package needs a licence and security review that takes weeks. Plan: (1) Default - solve it with the standard library. (2) Declared dependencies (fastapi, sqlalchemy, pytest) may be used as they are. (3) Not allowed - adding a package to pyproject.toml, or importing an undeclared one, without asking first. (4) If a package is truly needed, stop and ask, with the reason. (5) Considered: allowing small utility packages freely (rejected: the review cost is per package, not per size).

seed_decisions.title: Keep audit entries for 90 days
seed_decisions.content: Keep audit entries for 90 days, because the #93 compliance review raised the retention requirement; this replaces the earlier 30-day rule.

history.title: Keep audit entries for 30 days
history.content: Keep audit entries for 30 days, because audit storage was capped at the time.

variants.title: Return structured results as plain dicts
variants.content: Return structured results from public functions (a record, a summary) as plain dicts, never dataclasses, NamedTuples or other custom objects, because the JSON layer serialises results without adapters.

variants.title: Annotate public signatures with built-in generics and return plain dicts
variants.content: Type-annotate every public function signature in app/svc_{seed}_core.py with built-in generics (list[int], dict) rather than typing.List or typing.Dict, because the codebase targets Python 3.12 and mypy runs in strict mode on app/. Return structured results such as records and summaries as plain dicts, not TypedDict or dataclasses, so the JSON layer can serialise them without adapters.

variants.title: Return structured results as plain dicts in every public function
variants.content: Return structured results as plain dicts from public functions in the record service, because the gateway serialises results directly with json.dumps. Plan: (1) Return type - a record or summary is a built-in dict, annotated as dict; scalars and lists stay as they are. (2) Not allowed - dataclasses, NamedTuple, Pydantic models or custom classes as return values. (3) Internal helpers may use any structure, converted to a dict at the public boundary. (4) Annotations use built-in generics (list[int], dict). (5) Considered: dataclasses for readability (rejected: every gateway route would need an adapter, as #61 showed).

seed_decisions.title: Accept record ids up to 1,000,000
seed_decisions.content: Accept record ids from 1 up to 1,000,000, because the #90 storage migration widened the id space; the old 10,000 ceiling no longer applies.

history.title: Keep record ids below 10,000
history.content: Treat record ids of 10,000 or more as invalid, because the old storage tables were sized for 10,000 rows.

variants.title: Serialise hashed payloads with sorted, compact JSON
variants.content: Serialise anything that is hashed or compared with json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')), because key order changed between runs and broke the export job's dedup hash.

variants.title: Serialise compared or hashed payloads with sorted-key json.dumps
variants.content: Serialise payloads with json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')) whenever the record service writes something that is compared or hashed later, because key order changed between runs and broke the dedup hash in the export job. Plain json.dumps is fine for debug output. Don't hand-build JSON strings with f-strings; escaping bugs with ids containing quotes were the reason this came up. The export job hashes the serialised payload to skip unchanged rows; when two workers produced different key orders for the same record, every row looked changed and the nightly export re-sent the whole table (#52).

variants.title: Use one canonical JSON form for hashed or compared payloads
variants.content: Use one canonical JSON form for anything hashed or compared, because two workers produced different key orders for the same record and the export re-sent the whole table (#52). Plan: (1) Form - json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')), UTF-8 encoded before hashing. (2) Scope - digests, dedup keys, cache keys built from payloads, and any comparison of serialised records. (3) Not allowed - plain json.dumps, str(dict) or hand-built JSON strings for these uses. (4) Debug output may use any readable form. (5) Tests - assert that two dicts with different key order give the same digest.

variants.title: Use epoch-millisecond 'at_ms' timestamps
variants.content: Store timestamps as integer epoch milliseconds under 'at_ms', never datetime objects or ISO strings, because the dashboard client is JavaScript.

variants.title: Represent times as integer epoch milliseconds under 'at_ms'
variants.content: Represent times in app/svc_{seed}_core.py payloads as integer Unix epoch milliseconds under the key 'at_ms', because the dashboard and the export job disagreed about time zones. Until #71 the module mixed datetime objects (which json.dumps can't serialise, so callers stringified them inconsistently) and ISO-8601 strings, some with offsets and some naive. A daylight-saving change shifted a day of audit data by an hour and nobody could tell which rows were affected. We chose milliseconds over seconds because the JS client uses Date.now() natively, and an int over a float so equality checks in tests are exact. The field is always 'at_ms', not 'timestamp', 'ts' or 'created_at', so the client finds it without per-endpoint mapping. Existing ISO-string endpoints were left alone for now because two external consumers parse them; anything new uses 'at_ms'. Follow-up to migrate the old endpoints is tracked in #74.

variants.title: Standardise time representation across the record service
variants.content: Standardise time representation across the record service, because mixed formats corrupted an audit export. Plan: (1) Wire format - every timestamp the module returns is an int of Unix epoch milliseconds. (2) Key - the field is named 'at_ms' wherever a single event time is recorded, such as audit entries and change events. (3) Not allowed - datetime objects, ISO-8601 strings and float seconds. (4) Source - read the clock with time.time() or time.time_ns() at the moment the entry is built; never capture it at import. (5) Display formatting is the client's job. (6) Migration - existing endpoints that return ISO strings stay until their consumers move; new functions use 'at_ms' from day one. Discussed: RFC 3339 strings for readability (rejected: parsing cost and zone ambiguity in the JS client) and seconds (rejected: the client wants milliseconds). Testing note: compare 'at_ms' against time.time() * 1000 with a tolerance rather than freezing the clock, since the module has no clock injection and adding one was judged not worth it. Sign-off from the dashboard owner and the export-job owner on 2026-08-19.

prompt: Add list_slots_page(offset, limit) to app/svc_{seed}_core.py: a paged listing of the module's slot numbers (0 to 24) in order, with default arguments. Run the tests.
check_cmd: uv run python -c "import inspect; import app.svc_{seed}_core as m; p = inspect.signature(m.list_slots_page).parameters; assert p['offset'].default == 0 and p['limit'].default == 20, p; assert m.list_slots_page() == list(range(20)), m.list_slots_page()"
functional_cmd: uv run python -c "import app.svc_{seed}_core as m; assert m.list_slots_page(5, 3) == [5, 6, 7]; assert m.list_slots_page(23, 10) == [23, 24]"

variants.title: Keep the record service synchronous and single-threaded
variants.content: Keep the record service synchronous: no threads, asyncio or process pools inside the module, because the #41 async trial doubled latency variance; scale with more worker processes.

variants.title: Keep the record service synchronous and single-process
variants.content: Keep the record service synchronous and single-process, because the async rewrite attempted in #41 doubled latency variance without improving throughput. The rewrite moved the fetchers to asyncio with an aiohttp client and an async test runner. What we found: (1) the fetchers do no network I/O of their own, so the event loop only added scheduling overhead; (2) the test suite needed pytest-asyncio and every helper grew an async twin, roughly doubling the code to review; (3) tracing got harder because stack traces lost the caller. It was reverted after two weeks. If more concurrency is needed later, run more worker processes behind the queue instead of adding threads or async inside the module. Even for slow upstream reads, scale with more worker processes, not threads. Numbers from the trial, for the record: p50 latency was unchanged, p99 roughly doubled under the soak test because of event-loop starvation when one handler did CPU work, and throughput was flat because the bottleneck was the queue consumer, not the fetchers. (4) Two contributors spent most of the trial chasing a deadlock that came from mixing sync and async calls in one request path. The rewrite branch is kept for reference but should not be revived without a new benchmark showing I/O-bound fetchers. Agreed by the service owners on 2026-05-28.

variants.title: Keep concurrency out of the record service module
variants.content: Keep concurrency out of the record service module, because the #41 async rewrite doubled p99 latency without improving throughput. Plan: (1) Execution - fetchers and helpers run synchronously in the caller's thread. (2) Not allowed - threading, concurrent.futures, asyncio and multiprocessing inside app/, even around slow upstream reads. (3) Throughput - scale by running more worker processes behind the queue, which the platform already supports. (4) Speed-ups inside the module come from doing less work, for example the bounded cache, not from parallelism.

seed_decisions.title: Write tests as plain functions with bare asserts
seed_decisions.content: Write tests as plain functions with bare asserts in tests/test_svc_{seed}.py, because the suite should be readable without pytest knowledge; no classes, fixtures or parametrize unless a test genuinely needs them. Name each test test_<function>_<case>.

seed_decisions.title: Treat app/ as one synchronous record service with generated per-slot fetchers
seed_decisions.content: Treat app/ as one small synchronous record service with generated per-slot fetchers, because every convention in this repo assumes that structure. How it fits together, as worked out while answering a question about where new code should go: each app/svc_<n>_core.py module belongs to one numbered service and is generated from a template, which is why it holds a run of near-identical fetch_record_<n>_<slot> functions that each return a small record dict with an id and a slot. The slot number is positional and other systems depend on it, so generated functions are never renamed or renumbered. Hand-written code is added to the same module below the generated block; there is no separate package for helpers, and adding one was rejected as a layer with a single user. The module imports json and os but uses neither in the generated block; they are there for hand-written additions (serialisation for the export job, environment lookups). There is no web framework in this repository: the HTTP layer lives in the gateway, which calls these functions in-process, and the tests call them directly. Tests live in tests/test_svc_<n>.py, one file per service, as plain functions; the generated tests are placeholders that only prove the test runner works, so any real behaviour needs its own test. The service is deliberately synchronous (see the async decision) and keeps no state beyond bounded caches and the module-level metrics counters. Data flows one way: gateway calls a fetcher, the fetcher builds a dict, the gateway serialises it. Nothing in app/ talks to a database directly yet; the record dicts are synthetic until the storage migration (#80) lands, which is why fetchers are trivial today. When adding a feature, the questions to ask are which service module owns it, whether it changes the record shape (it should not), and whether it needs a test in that service's test file (it does). Anything cross-service belongs in the gateway, not here. This summary was written on 2026-09-02 and anchored to app/ so it is flagged as stale if the layout changes.

seed_decisions.title: Raise RecordGone for deleted records
seed_decisions.content: Deleted records must raise RecordGone; callers kept treating tombstone dicts as live records, so never return one.

seed_decisions.title: Show slot identifiers like SLOT_07
seed_decisions.content: Slot identifiers shown to operators use the SLOT_07 form (upper case, underscore), matching the keys the ops runbook uses for alerts.

seed_decisions.title: Label slots like slot-07
seed_decisions.content: Label slots in lowercase with a dash and two digits, like slot-07, because the dashboard builds its page URLs from the label.
Public functions in app/svc_{seed}_core.py keep a one-line docstring that names the service number.

variants.title: Return partial results from batch record lookups
variants.content: Batch record lookups return partial results: the good records under 'items' and the rejected ids (anything below 1) under 'failed'. Don't raise on a bad id mid-batch, because the caller retries only the failures. fetch_records_legacy predates this rule and raises on the first bad id; it stays only for the old export path, so new code must not copy it.

variants.title: Return partial results from batch lookups instead of failing the whole call
variants.content: Return partial results from batch lookups in app/svc_{seed}_core.py instead of failing the whole call, because the reporting client retries only the ids that failed. This came out of #58: the first batch helper looped over fetch_record_{seed}_0 and raised on the first id below 1, so a nightly export of 4,000 ids died on one bad row and the client re-sent all 4,000. We considered returning None per slot but rejected it, since None was ambiguous between 'not found' and 'invalid'. The shape agreed with the client team was a dict with two keys: 'items', holding the record dicts in the usual {'id', 'slot'} shape, and 'failed', holding the ids that were rejected. Invalid means an id below 1; those are reported, not raised, and the loop carries on. Anything that wraps several record fetches should follow the same shape so the client only needs one parser. The client's retry job reads 'failed' verbatim and re-queues those ids after the upstream fix, so the ids must come back exactly as passed in, not normalised or stringified. Raised in standup on 2026-08-04, agreed with the client team the same week. fetch_records_legacy predates this decision and is kept only for the old export path until it migrates (#58); don't model new batch code on it, since it aborts on the first bad id.

variants.title: Adopt a partial-result contract for multi-record reads
variants.content: Adopt a partial-result contract for multi-record reads in the record service, because callers need to retry failures without redoing successful reads. Plan approved 2026-08-12 for the batch work: (1) Scope - any function in app/svc_{seed}_core.py that takes a list of ids from the caller and reads them; the single-record fetch_record_{seed}_N functions are unchanged. (2) Return type - a dict, never a bare list or generator, so the contract can grow later without breaking callers. It carries 'items' (the records that were read, each in the existing record shape) and 'failed' (the ids that could not be read). (3) Validation - an id below 1 is rejected up front and appended to 'failed'; it must not raise and must not stop the remaining ids from being read. (4) Ordering - 'items' follows the order of the input ids. (5) Out of scope - pagination, async fan-out and per-id error messages were discussed and deferred to a follow-up issue. (6) Tests - each batch function gets a test that mixes valid and invalid ids, and one where every id is invalid, which must return an empty 'items' rather than raising. (7) Logging - the existing rule applies: report how many ids failed, never which ones. (8) Documentation - the docstring states the partial-result behaviour in one line so callers don't have to read the body. Owner: the record-service maintainers; the client team signs off on any change to the two key names, since they are part of the wire contract. (7) Legacy - fetch_records_legacy keeps its old raise-on-first-bad-id behaviour for the export path until that path migrates; new multi-record functions follow this contract, not it.

variants.title: Keep counters in a module-level metrics dict
variants.content: Count things in a module-level dict keyed by snake_case metric names that start with svc_ and end with _total (for example svc_records_fetched_total), because the /metrics endpoint renders that dict.

variants.title: Expose counters through the existing /metrics endpoint
variants.content: Expose counters through the existing /metrics endpoint rather than adding a metrics library, because the platform team scrapes only that endpoint. Counters live in a module-level dict keyed by metric name and reset only on process start. This was chosen over prometheus_client in #60, since that would have been a new dependency and a second exposition format to maintain. Cache hit ratios are read from cache_info() on the cached functions, so keep those functions at module level where the endpoint can find them. Naming: snake_case counter names prefixed with the service, for example svc_records_fetched_total; the endpoint renders them in the Prometheus text format by hand, which has been enough so far. Don't add gauges for things the platform already measures (CPU, memory).

variants.title: Expose service counters through the module-level metrics dict
variants.content: Expose service counters through a module-level metrics dict, because the platform team scrapes only the existing /metrics endpoint. Plan from #60: (1) Storage - counters live in a module-level dict keyed by metric name, which the endpoint reads. (2) Names - snake_case, starting with svc_ and ending with _total for counts, for example svc_records_fetched_total. (3) Updates - increment in the function that does the work; reset only on process start. (4) Not allowed - prometheus_client or another metrics library (a new dependency), and bare module-level integers the endpoint cannot see. (5) Platform metrics such as CPU and memory are not duplicated here.

seed_decisions.title: Return a JSON status from health()
seed_decisions.content: Make health() return {'status': 'ok'}, because the monitoring stack parses the body as JSON.

seed_decisions.title: Cap batch calls at 500 ids
seed_decisions.content: Cap batch calls at 500 ids and raise ValueError above that, because the #95 load test showed the workers handle 500 comfortably; this replaces the 100-id cap.

history.title: Cap batch calls at 100 ids
history.content: Cap batch calls at 100 ids and raise ValueError above that, because larger batches timed out at the gateway.

variants.title: Raise RecordInputError for ids below 1
variants.content: Single-record fetches raise RecordInputError, a ValueError subclass that lives in the service module (add it if it isn't there yet), for an id below 1. Don't return None or an error dict, because callers catch the exception type.

variants.title: Signal bad input from single-record fetchers with RecordInputError
variants.content: Signal bad input from single-record fetchers with a dedicated RecordInputError, a ValueError subclass that belongs in app/svc_{seed}_core.py, because callers need to tell invalid ids apart from other failures. Review of #66 found three conventions in use: some fetchers returned None for id 0, one returned {'error': 'bad id'}, and one raised a bare ValueError. The None case was silently cached downstream as 'record not found'. Agreed outcome: ids below 1 raise RecordInputError, and subclassing ValueError keeps existing except ValueError handlers working. Batch helpers are the exception and report bad ids in their 'failed' list instead. The class hadn't been added when the review closed; the first change that needs it should define it at module level. Message text: the id may appear in the exception so the caller can report it, but keep it out of logs per the logging rule. Tests should assert the exception type, not the message, so wording can change freely.

variants.title: Define one exception type for invalid input to record fetchers
variants.content: Define one exception type for invalid input to the record fetchers, because mixed None, error-dict and ValueError returns were leaking into caches. Plan: (1) Add class RecordInputError(ValueError) at module level in app/svc_{seed}_core.py. (2) Single-record functions (fetch_record_{seed}_N and similar) raise it for any id below 1, before doing any work. (3) Never return None or an error dict to signal bad input. (4) Batch functions don't raise; they follow the partial-result contract. (5) The offending id may appear in the exception message but never in logs; the logging rule still applies. (6) Tests cover id 0 and a negative id. Alternatives: returning Optional (rejected: ambiguous with not-found) and a Result type (rejected: unidiomatic in this codebase). (7) Rollout - the first fetcher to validate its input introduces the class; the rest adopt it as they are touched, rather than in one sweeping change, to keep diffs reviewable. (8) Callers that currently check for None after a fetch keep working until their fetcher is migrated, then switch to catching RecordInputError.

variants.title: Never log record ids or function arguments
variants.content: Never log record ids or function arguments from the record service, because compliance treats request data as customer data; log counts and durations instead.

variants.title: Never log record ids or function arguments
variants.content: Never log record ids or function arguments in app/svc_{seed}_core.py, because compliance classifies request data as customer data and the log pipeline isn't approved for it (audit finding, June 2026). That includes debug logs and messages passed to logger.exception; log counts and durations instead. If an error needs an id to be debuggable, put it in the exception for the caller to handle, not in a log line. The audit sampled two weeks of logs and found ids in debug output from three modules; this one was cleaned up first. Applies to print() as well, since stdout is shipped to the same pipeline.

variants.title: Keep request data out of the record service's logs
variants.content: Keep request data out of the record service's logs, because the June 2026 audit classified record ids as customer data. Plan: (1) Never log record ids, function arguments or returned records, at any level, including debug. (2) Log what operators need without request data: that a call happened, counts and durations. (3) Exceptions may carry an id for the caller, but logger.exception messages must not include it. (4) print() follows the same rule, since stdout ships to the same pipeline. (5) Use the module logger, logging.getLogger(__name__), so levels can be set per module.

seed_decisions.title: Return a tombstone for deleted records
seed_decisions.content: Return a tombstone, {'id': record_id, 'deleted': True}, for deleted records instead of raising, because the export job counts tombstones to reconcile deletions.

seed_decisions.title: Name hand-written functions verb_noun without the slot suffix
seed_decisions.content: Name new hand-written public functions verb_noun (for example build_report or list_slots) and keep the service-number suffix only on the generated per-slot fetchers, because the slot registry parses the generated names and hand-written names must not collide with that pattern.

seed_decisions.title: Prefix versions with v
seed_decisions.content: Prefix version strings with a lowercase v, as in v1.4.0, so they match the git tags exactly.

variants.title: Bound every cache at 256 entries
variants.content: Use functools.lru_cache(maxsize=256) for any memoisation in the record service, never an unbounded cache, because the worker runs on a fixed memory budget.

variants.title: Cap caches with lru_cache(maxsize=256) after the OOM incident
variants.content: Cap caches in app/svc_{seed}_core.py with functools.lru_cache(maxsize=256), because an unbounded cache took the worker down. In August a dict-based cache was added around the record fetchers to speed up the dashboard; it never evicted, grew to several hundred MB over a week, and the container was OOM-killed (#63). functools.cache and lru_cache(maxsize=None) have the same problem, so both were ruled out in review. 256 entries covered the dashboard's hot set, judging by the access logs at the time. If a function needs caching, wrap it with lru_cache(maxsize=256) directly so cache_info() stays available to the metrics endpoint. A per-call dict passed in by the caller is fine for request-scoped reuse; the rule is about anything that outlives a call. Raised again in review of #67, where a contributor reached for functools.cache because it is shorter; the reviewer pointed back here.

variants.title: Introduce bounded memoisation for record reads
variants.content: Introduce bounded memoisation for record reads, because repeated reads of the same ids dominate dashboard latency. Plan: (1) Mechanism - functools.lru_cache from the standard library; no third-party cache and no hand-rolled dict, since eviction is the part that is easy to get wrong. (2) Size - maxsize=256 for every cache in app/svc_{seed}_core.py; an unbounded size (maxsize=None, functools.cache) is not allowed. (3) Observability - keep the cache object reachable at module level so cache_info() can be scraped; don't hide it inside a closure. (4) Invalidation - records are immutable for a given id, so no TTL is needed now; revisit if records become writable. (5) Rollout - start with the hottest fetchers, measure, then extend. Alternatives considered: a Redis cache (rejected: new infrastructure for a single process) and cachetools.TTLCache (rejected: a new dependency for no current need). Risks noted at sign-off: memoising a function that returns a mutable dict lets one caller's mutation leak to the next, so callers must treat cached records as read-only; and a cache on a function that raises caches nothing, which is the behaviour we want for invalid ids. The 256 figure is per cache, not shared across the module.

variants.title: Fail fast in fetchers; let the client retry
variants.content: Fetchers make one upstream attempt and fail fast on a timeout; never add retry loops inside them, because the client already retries and nested retries caused the #55 request storm.

variants.title: Keep retries out of fetchers after the #55 request storm
variants.content: Don't put retry loops inside the fetch functions in app/svc_{seed}_core.py; retries belong to the client layer, because nested retries in #55 turned one slow dependency into a nine-fold request storm. During that incident the client retried three times, the gateway retried three times, and a fetcher wrapped its own call in a three-attempt loop, so one slow upstream received nine requests per user action and fell over completely. The post-incident review assigned retry ownership to the client, which also owns the backoff policy. A fetcher makes at most one upstream call; on a timeout it fails fast with a typed error the client's retry policy can recognise.

variants.title: Make record fetchers fail fast instead of retrying
variants.content: Make record fetchers fail fast instead of retrying, because the client owns retries and backoff. Plan from the #55 post-incident review: (1) One attempt - each fetcher in app/svc_{seed}_core.py calls the upstream at most once per invocation. (2) No loops - no retry, backoff or sleep inside fetchers, including a single extra attempt. (3) Typed failure - on a timeout, raise a module-level error the client can match, instead of returning None or a placeholder record. (4) Ownership - retry count and backoff live in the client's policy, so they can be tuned in one place. (5) Considered: a small in-fetcher retry with jitter (rejected: it multiplies with client and gateway retries, which is exactly what caused the storm).

seed_decisions.title: Manage dependencies and commands with uv
seed_decisions.content: Use uv for every dependency and script command in this repo (uv sync, uv run pytest), never pip or a bare python, because uv.lock is the source of truth and pip installs drift from it. CI runs uv sync --frozen and fails if the lock is stale.

seed_decisions.title: Return the plain string OK from health()
seed_decisions.content: The load balancer expects the literal body OK from the health check; return the plain string 'OK' and nothing else.

variants.title: Keep fetchers as plain module functions
variants.content: Expose record lookups as module-level functions (or a dict of them), never a repository, service or manager class, because #77's RecordRepository duplicated every function. Exception classes are fine.

variants.title: Don't wrap the fetchers in a class layer
variants.content: Keep app/svc_{seed}_core.py a module of plain functions and don't add a repository, service or manager class over the fetchers, because the RecordRepository introduced in #77 duplicated every fetcher as a method and was removed two months later. Every caller then had to construct an object it did not need, and the class and the functions drifted apart. Callers import functions directly; a dispatch table (a dict from slot to function) is fine when a lookup by slot is needed. Exception classes and plain data are not affected by this rule.

variants.title: Adopt a no-class-layer rule for the record service
variants.content: Adopt a no-class-layer rule for the record service, because an interface with one implementation added code without adding behaviour. Plan: (1) Public API - module-level functions only. (2) Lookups - a function, or a dict mapping keys to functions, never an object with methods. (3) Not allowed - repository, service, manager or client classes wrapping the fetchers, including singletons. (4) Allowed - exception classes. (5) Revisit only if a second storage backend actually exists.

variants.title: Write files atomically with mode 0o600
variants.content: Write every file the record service produces to a temp file in the same directory and os.replace it into place with mode 0o600, because a crash mid-write left a truncated export the importer accepted.

variants.title: Replace output files atomically after the truncated export
variants.content: Replace output files atomically in app/svc_{seed}_core.py: write to a temporary file in the destination's directory, then os.replace it over the target, because a worker killed mid-write in #84 left a half-written export that the importer accepted as complete. Writing in place meant readers could see a partial file at any moment, and a crash left it that way. The temp file must live in the same directory so os.replace stays an atomic rename on one filesystem. Exports hold customer records, so the final file has mode 0o600, readable only by the service user; the default umask produced world-readable files.

variants.title: Adopt atomic, private writes for service output files
variants.content: Adopt atomic, private writes for every file the record service writes, because partial and world-readable exports both caused incidents. Plan: (1) Temp file - create it in the target's directory (tempfile.mkstemp with dir=), so the final rename stays on one filesystem. (2) Write and flush the full content to the temp file. (3) Replace - os.replace(temp, target); never write the target in place. (4) Permissions - the result is mode 0o600. (5) Cleanup - remove the temp file if writing fails, so no stray files are left. (6) Considered: writing in place with fsync (rejected: readers can still see a partial file).

seed_decisions.title: Treat calls over 150 ms as slow
seed_decisions.content: Treat an upstream call that takes more than 150 ms as slow, because the #99 latency review tightened the earlier 200 ms threshold.

history.title: Treat calls over 200 ms as slow
history.content: Treat an upstream call that takes more than 200 ms as slow, because that matched the gateway's alerting at the time.

variants.title: Read configuration at call time, never at import
variants.content: Read settings from os.environ inside the function that needs them, never at import time, because the test runner and the worker set variables after import.

variants.title: Never read configuration at import time
variants.content: Never read configuration at import time in the service modules; read os.environ inside the function that needs it, because the test runner and the worker set environment variables after import and import-time reads froze stale values (this bit us twice with the region setting). Secrets never go in code or in default values. Tests that need a setting use monkeypatch.setenv inside the test, which only works because nothing reads the variable at import. Defaults for non-secret settings live next to the read, as the second argument to os.environ.get.

variants.title: Read configuration at call time in every service module
variants.content: Read configuration at call time in every service module, because import-time reads froze stale values twice. Plan from the region-setting incidents: (1) Where - os.environ is read inside the function that uses the value, on every call. (2) Defaults - a non-secret default sits next to the read as the second argument to os.environ.get; secrets have no default. (3) Not allowed - module-level constants computed from the environment, and caching a setting at import. (4) Tests - set variables with monkeypatch.setenv inside the test, which only works because nothing reads them at import. (5) Considered: a settings object loaded once at startup (rejected: it brings back the stale-value problem for the worker).

seed_decisions.title: Publish bare semantic versions
seed_decisions.content: Publish versions as bare semantic versions such as 1.4.0; the package index rejects a leading letter.

seed_decisions.title: Test every new public function before finishing
seed_decisions.content: Every new public function in app/ needs at least one test before the change is finished, and run uv run pytest tests/ -q before reporting done, because CI blocks merges on missing tests for new symbols.

variants.title: Never write back after a forgiving read
variants.content: Use a forgiving reader (one that turns a corrupt file into []) only for display; a function that writes the file back must load it with a reader that raises on corruption, because a forgiving read before a write wiped a queued export.

variants.title: Load strictly before writing after the wiped export
variants.content: Load files strictly in any function that writes them back, because a forgiving read before a write replaced a queued export with an empty list in #86. load_records in app/svc_{seed}_core.py deliberately reads a corrupt or unreadable file as empty, which is right for the dashboard: showing nothing beats crashing. But an append built on it read the damaged file as [], added one record and saved, silently discarding everything that was there. Display paths keep the forgiving reader; write paths parse with json.load and let the decode error propagate, so a human can recover the file. A missing file may still be treated as empty.

variants.title: Separate forgiving reads from strict reads before writes
variants.content: Separate forgiving reads from strict reads, because a corrupt file read as empty before a write erased queued data. Plan: (1) Display paths may use a reader that returns [] for a corrupt or unreadable file. (2) Any function that writes a file back loads it with a strict parser and lets a decode error propagate; it never writes after a failed parse. (3) A missing file may be treated as empty on both paths. (4) Tests cover a corrupt file on every write path and assert the file is untouched. (5) Considered: backing up the file before every write (rejected: it hides the corruption instead of surfacing it).

seed_decisions.title: Keep the record dict shape stable for per-slot fetchers
seed_decisions.content: Keep the record dict shape {'id': ..., 'slot': ...} stable for every fetch_record_{seed}_N function, because the export job and two dashboards index into it by key and break on extra or renamed fields. In #49 someone added a 'source' field to three fetchers, and the export job's strict schema check rejected every row for a day before anyone noticed. If a caller needs more data, add a separate function that returns a new shape rather than widening the record. Slot numbers are positional and stable: fetch_record_{seed}_7 always returns slot 7, so never renumber functions when one is removed; leave a gap instead. The export job's schema lives in another repository and is versioned separately, so even an additive field needs a coordinated release there first; that coordination cost is why new data goes into new functions. The incident write-up is linked from #49; the follow-up added a schema-contract test on the export side, not here.

variants.title: Use the standard library before any third-party package
variants.content: Use the standard library before any third-party package, and don't add a dependency to pyproject.toml without asking, because each new package needs a licence and security review.

variants.title: Ask before adding third-party dependencies
variants.content: Do not add third-party dependencies to the record service without asking first; prefer the standard library (functools, json, time, datetime), because every new package needs a licence and security review that takes weeks.

variants.title: Keep the record service on the standard library unless a dependency is approved
variants.content: Keep the record service on the standard library unless a dependency is approved, because every new package needs a licence and security review that takes weeks. Plan: (1) Default - solve it with the standard library. (2) Declared dependencies (fastapi, sqlalchemy, pytest) may be used as they are. (3) Not allowed - adding a package to pyproject.toml, or importing an undeclared one, without asking first. (4) If a package is truly needed, stop and ask, with the reason. (5) Considered: allowing small utility packages freely (rejected: the review cost is per package, not per size).

seed_decisions.title: Keep audit entries for 90 days
seed_decisions.content: Keep audit entries for 90 days, because the #93 compliance review raised the retention requirement; this replaces the earlier 30-day rule.

history.title: Keep audit entries for 30 days
history.content: Keep audit entries for 30 days, because audit storage was capped at the time.

variants.title: Return structured results as plain dicts
variants.content: Return structured results from public functions (a record, a summary) as plain dicts, never dataclasses, NamedTuples or other custom objects, because the JSON layer serialises results without adapters.

variants.title: Annotate public signatures with built-in generics and return plain dicts
variants.content: Type-annotate every public function signature in app/svc_{seed}_core.py with built-in generics (list[int], dict) rather than typing.List or typing.Dict, because the codebase targets Python 3.12 and mypy runs in strict mode on app/. Return structured results such as records and summaries as plain dicts, not TypedDict or dataclasses, so the JSON layer can serialise them without adapters.

variants.title: Return structured results as plain dicts in every public function
variants.content: Return structured results as plain dicts from public functions in the record service, because the gateway serialises results directly with json.dumps. Plan: (1) Return type - a record or summary is a built-in dict, annotated as dict; scalars and lists stay as they are. (2) Not allowed - dataclasses, NamedTuple, Pydantic models or custom classes as return values. (3) Internal helpers may use any structure, converted to a dict at the public boundary. (4) Annotations use built-in generics (list[int], dict). (5) Considered: dataclasses for readability (rejected: every gateway route would need an adapter, as #61 showed).

seed_decisions.title: Accept record ids up to 1,000,000
seed_decisions.content: Accept record ids from 1 up to 1,000,000, because the #90 storage migration widened the id space; the old 10,000 ceiling no longer applies.

history.title: Keep record ids below 10,000
history.content: Treat record ids of 10,000 or more as invalid, because the old storage tables were sized for 10,000 rows.

variants.title: Serialise hashed payloads with sorted, compact JSON
variants.content: Serialise anything that is hashed or compared with json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')), because key order changed between runs and broke the export job's dedup hash.

variants.title: Serialise compared or hashed payloads with sorted-key json.dumps
variants.content: Serialise payloads with json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')) whenever the record service writes something that is compared or hashed later, because key order changed between runs and broke the dedup hash in the export job. Plain json.dumps is fine for debug output. Don't hand-build JSON strings with f-strings; escaping bugs with ids containing quotes were the reason this came up. The export job hashes the serialised payload to skip unchanged rows; when two workers produced different key orders for the same record, every row looked changed and the nightly export re-sent the whole table (#52).

variants.title: Use one canonical JSON form for hashed or compared payloads
variants.content: Use one canonical JSON form for anything hashed or compared, because two workers produced different key orders for the same record and the export re-sent the whole table (#52). Plan: (1) Form - json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')), UTF-8 encoded before hashing. (2) Scope - digests, dedup keys, cache keys built from payloads, and any comparison of serialised records. (3) Not allowed - plain json.dumps, str(dict) or hand-built JSON strings for these uses. (4) Debug output may use any readable form. (5) Tests - assert that two dicts with different key order give the same digest.

variants.title: Use epoch-millisecond 'at_ms' timestamps
variants.content: Store timestamps as integer epoch milliseconds under 'at_ms', never datetime objects or ISO strings, because the dashboard client is JavaScript.

variants.title: Represent times as integer epoch milliseconds under 'at_ms'
variants.content: Represent times in app/svc_{seed}_core.py payloads as integer Unix epoch milliseconds under the key 'at_ms', because the dashboard and the export job disagreed about time zones. Until #71 the module mixed datetime objects (which json.dumps can't serialise, so callers stringified them inconsistently) and ISO-8601 strings, some with offsets and some naive. A daylight-saving change shifted a day of audit data by an hour and nobody could tell which rows were affected. We chose milliseconds over seconds because the JS client uses Date.now() natively, and an int over a float so equality checks in tests are exact. The field is always 'at_ms', not 'timestamp', 'ts' or 'created_at', so the client finds it without per-endpoint mapping. Existing ISO-string endpoints were left alone for now because two external consumers parse them; anything new uses 'at_ms'. Follow-up to migrate the old endpoints is tracked in #74.

variants.title: Standardise time representation across the record service
variants.content: Standardise time representation across the record service, because mixed formats corrupted an audit export. Plan: (1) Wire format - every timestamp the module returns is an int of Unix epoch milliseconds. (2) Key - the field is named 'at_ms' wherever a single event time is recorded, such as audit entries and change events. (3) Not allowed - datetime objects, ISO-8601 strings and float seconds. (4) Source - read the clock with time.time() or time.time_ns() at the moment the entry is built; never capture it at import. (5) Display formatting is the client's job. (6) Migration - existing endpoints that return ISO strings stay until their consumers move; new functions use 'at_ms' from day one. Discussed: RFC 3339 strings for readability (rejected: parsing cost and zone ambiguity in the JS client) and seconds (rejected: the client wants milliseconds). Testing note: compare 'at_ms' against time.time() * 1000 with a tolerance rather than freezing the clock, since the module has no clock injection and adding one was judged not worth it. Sign-off from the dashboard owner and the export-job owner on 2026-08-19.

prompt: Add a function records_region() -> str to app/svc_{seed}_core.py that returns the deployment region from the SVC_REGION environment variable, defaulting to 'eu-west-1'. Add a test and run the tests.
check_cmd: uv run python -c "import os; os.environ.pop('SVC_REGION', None); import app.svc_{seed}_core as m; os.environ['SVC_REGION'] = 'ap-south-1'; assert m.records_region() == 'ap-south-1', m.records_region()"
functional_cmd: uv run python -c "import importlib, os; os.environ['SVC_REGION'] = 'us-east-2'; import app.svc_{seed}_core as m; assert m.records_region() == 'us-east-2'; del os.environ['SVC_REGION']; importlib.reload(m); assert m.records_region() == 'eu-west-1', m.records_region()"

fixture_files.content:
# svc-{seed} record service

Record fetchers for service {seed}.

## Development

```bash
uv sync
uv run pytest tests/ -q
```

## Configuration

Settings come from environment variables and are read inside the function that needs them, at
call time, never at import: the test runner and the worker set variables after import.
Non-secret defaults go next to the read, as the second argument to `os.environ.get`.

variants.title: Keep the record service synchronous and single-threaded
variants.content: Keep the record service synchronous: no threads, asyncio or process pools inside the module, because the #41 async trial doubled latency variance; scale with more worker processes.

variants.title: Keep the record service synchronous and single-process
variants.content: Keep the record service synchronous and single-process, because the async rewrite attempted in #41 doubled latency variance without improving throughput. The rewrite moved the fetchers to asyncio with an aiohttp client and an async test runner. What we found: (1) the fetchers do no network I/O of their own, so the event loop only added scheduling overhead; (2) the test suite needed pytest-asyncio and every helper grew an async twin, roughly doubling the code to review; (3) tracing got harder because stack traces lost the caller. It was reverted after two weeks. If more concurrency is needed later, run more worker processes behind the queue instead of adding threads or async inside the module. Even for slow upstream reads, scale with more worker processes, not threads. Numbers from the trial, for the record: p50 latency was unchanged, p99 roughly doubled under the soak test because of event-loop starvation when one handler did CPU work, and throughput was flat because the bottleneck was the queue consumer, not the fetchers. (4) Two contributors spent most of the trial chasing a deadlock that came from mixing sync and async calls in one request path. The rewrite branch is kept for reference but should not be revived without a new benchmark showing I/O-bound fetchers. Agreed by the service owners on 2026-05-28.

variants.title: Keep concurrency out of the record service module
variants.content: Keep concurrency out of the record service module, because the #41 async rewrite doubled p99 latency without improving throughput. Plan: (1) Execution - fetchers and helpers run synchronously in the caller's thread. (2) Not allowed - threading, concurrent.futures, asyncio and multiprocessing inside app/, even around slow upstream reads. (3) Throughput - scale by running more worker processes behind the queue, which the platform already supports. (4) Speed-ups inside the module come from doing less work, for example the bounded cache, not from parallelism.

seed_decisions.title: Write tests as plain functions with bare asserts
seed_decisions.content: Write tests as plain functions with bare asserts in tests/test_svc_{seed}.py, because the suite should be readable without pytest knowledge; no classes, fixtures or parametrize unless a test genuinely needs them. Name each test test_<function>_<case>.

seed_decisions.title: Treat app/ as one synchronous record service with generated per-slot fetchers
seed_decisions.content: Treat app/ as one small synchronous record service with generated per-slot fetchers, because every convention in this repo assumes that structure. How it fits together, as worked out while answering a question about where new code should go: each app/svc_<n>_core.py module belongs to one numbered service and is generated from a template, which is why it holds a run of near-identical fetch_record_<n>_<slot> functions that each return a small record dict with an id and a slot. The slot number is positional and other systems depend on it, so generated functions are never renamed or renumbered. Hand-written code is added to the same module below the generated block; there is no separate package for helpers, and adding one was rejected as a layer with a single user. The module imports json and os but uses neither in the generated block; they are there for hand-written additions (serialisation for the export job, environment lookups). There is no web framework in this repository: the HTTP layer lives in the gateway, which calls these functions in-process, and the tests call them directly. Tests live in tests/test_svc_<n>.py, one file per service, as plain functions; the generated tests are placeholders that only prove the test runner works, so any real behaviour needs its own test. The service is deliberately synchronous (see the async decision) and keeps no state beyond bounded caches and the module-level metrics counters. Data flows one way: gateway calls a fetcher, the fetcher builds a dict, the gateway serialises it. Nothing in app/ talks to a database directly yet; the record dicts are synthetic until the storage migration (#80) lands, which is why fetchers are trivial today. When adding a feature, the questions to ask are which service module owns it, whether it changes the record shape (it should not), and whether it needs a test in that service's test file (it does). Anything cross-service belongs in the gateway, not here. This summary was written on 2026-09-02 and anchored to app/ so it is flagged as stale if the layout changes.

seed_decisions.title: Raise RecordGone for deleted records
seed_decisions.content: Deleted records must raise RecordGone; callers kept treating tombstone dicts as live records, so never return one.

seed_decisions.title: Show slot identifiers like SLOT_07
seed_decisions.content: Slot identifiers shown to operators use the SLOT_07 form (upper case, underscore), matching the keys the ops runbook uses for alerts.

seed_decisions.title: Label slots like slot-07
seed_decisions.content: Label slots in lowercase with a dash and two digits, like slot-07, because the dashboard builds its page URLs from the label.
Public functions in app/svc_{seed}_core.py keep a one-line docstring that names the service number.

variants.title: Return partial results from batch record lookups
variants.content: Batch record lookups return partial results: the good records under 'items' and the rejected ids (anything below 1) under 'failed'. Don't raise on a bad id mid-batch, because the caller retries only the failures. fetch_records_legacy predates this rule and raises on the first bad id; it stays only for the old export path, so new code must not copy it.

variants.title: Return partial results from batch lookups instead of failing the whole call
variants.content: Return partial results from batch lookups in app/svc_{seed}_core.py instead of failing the whole call, because the reporting client retries only the ids that failed. This came out of #58: the first batch helper looped over fetch_record_{seed}_0 and raised on the first id below 1, so a nightly export of 4,000 ids died on one bad row and the client re-sent all 4,000. We considered returning None per slot but rejected it, since None was ambiguous between 'not found' and 'invalid'. The shape agreed with the client team was a dict with two keys: 'items', holding the record dicts in the usual {'id', 'slot'} shape, and 'failed', holding the ids that were rejected. Invalid means an id below 1; those are reported, not raised, and the loop carries on. Anything that wraps several record fetches should follow the same shape so the client only needs one parser. The client's retry job reads 'failed' verbatim and re-queues those ids after the upstream fix, so the ids must come back exactly as passed in, not normalised or stringified. Raised in standup on 2026-08-04, agreed with the client team the same week. fetch_records_legacy predates this decision and is kept only for the old export path until it migrates (#58); don't model new batch code on it, since it aborts on the first bad id.

variants.title: Adopt a partial-result contract for multi-record reads
variants.content: Adopt a partial-result contract for multi-record reads in the record service, because callers need to retry failures without redoing successful reads. Plan approved 2026-08-12 for the batch work: (1) Scope - any function in app/svc_{seed}_core.py that takes a list of ids from the caller and reads them; the single-record fetch_record_{seed}_N functions are unchanged. (2) Return type - a dict, never a bare list or generator, so the contract can grow later without breaking callers. It carries 'items' (the records that were read, each in the existing record shape) and 'failed' (the ids that could not be read). (3) Validation - an id below 1 is rejected up front and appended to 'failed'; it must not raise and must not stop the remaining ids from being read. (4) Ordering - 'items' follows the order of the input ids. (5) Out of scope - pagination, async fan-out and per-id error messages were discussed and deferred to a follow-up issue. (6) Tests - each batch function gets a test that mixes valid and invalid ids, and one where every id is invalid, which must return an empty 'items' rather than raising. (7) Logging - the existing rule applies: report how many ids failed, never which ones. (8) Documentation - the docstring states the partial-result behaviour in one line so callers don't have to read the body. Owner: the record-service maintainers; the client team signs off on any change to the two key names, since they are part of the wire contract. (7) Legacy - fetch_records_legacy keeps its old raise-on-first-bad-id behaviour for the export path until that path migrates; new multi-record functions follow this contract, not it.

variants.title: Keep counters in a module-level metrics dict
variants.content: Count things in a module-level dict keyed by snake_case metric names that start with svc_ and end with _total (for example svc_records_fetched_total), because the /metrics endpoint renders that dict.

variants.title: Expose counters through the existing /metrics endpoint
variants.content: Expose counters through the existing /metrics endpoint rather than adding a metrics library, because the platform team scrapes only that endpoint. Counters live in a module-level dict keyed by metric name and reset only on process start. This was chosen over prometheus_client in #60, since that would have been a new dependency and a second exposition format to maintain. Cache hit ratios are read from cache_info() on the cached functions, so keep those functions at module level where the endpoint can find them. Naming: snake_case counter names prefixed with the service, for example svc_records_fetched_total; the endpoint renders them in the Prometheus text format by hand, which has been enough so far. Don't add gauges for things the platform already measures (CPU, memory).

variants.title: Expose service counters through the module-level metrics dict
variants.content: Expose service counters through a module-level metrics dict, because the platform team scrapes only the existing /metrics endpoint. Plan from #60: (1) Storage - counters live in a module-level dict keyed by metric name, which the endpoint reads. (2) Names - snake_case, starting with svc_ and ending with _total for counts, for example svc_records_fetched_total. (3) Updates - increment in the function that does the work; reset only on process start. (4) Not allowed - prometheus_client or another metrics library (a new dependency), and bare module-level integers the endpoint cannot see. (5) Platform metrics such as CPU and memory are not duplicated here.

seed_decisions.title: Return a JSON status from health()
seed_decisions.content: Make health() return {'status': 'ok'}, because the monitoring stack parses the body as JSON.

seed_decisions.title: Cap batch calls at 500 ids
seed_decisions.content: Cap batch calls at 500 ids and raise ValueError above that, because the #95 load test showed the workers handle 500 comfortably; this replaces the 100-id cap.

history.title: Cap batch calls at 100 ids
history.content: Cap batch calls at 100 ids and raise ValueError above that, because larger batches timed out at the gateway.

variants.title: Raise RecordInputError for ids below 1
variants.content: Single-record fetches raise RecordInputError, a ValueError subclass that lives in the service module (add it if it isn't there yet), for an id below 1. Don't return None or an error dict, because callers catch the exception type.

variants.title: Signal bad input from single-record fetchers with RecordInputError
variants.content: Signal bad input from single-record fetchers with a dedicated RecordInputError, a ValueError subclass that belongs in app/svc_{seed}_core.py, because callers need to tell invalid ids apart from other failures. Review of #66 found three conventions in use: some fetchers returned None for id 0, one returned {'error': 'bad id'}, and one raised a bare ValueError. The None case was silently cached downstream as 'record not found'. Agreed outcome: ids below 1 raise RecordInputError, and subclassing ValueError keeps existing except ValueError handlers working. Batch helpers are the exception and report bad ids in their 'failed' list instead. The class hadn't been added when the review closed; the first change that needs it should define it at module level. Message text: the id may appear in the exception so the caller can report it, but keep it out of logs per the logging rule. Tests should assert the exception type, not the message, so wording can change freely.

variants.title: Define one exception type for invalid input to record fetchers
variants.content: Define one exception type for invalid input to the record fetchers, because mixed None, error-dict and ValueError returns were leaking into caches. Plan: (1) Add class RecordInputError(ValueError) at module level in app/svc_{seed}_core.py. (2) Single-record functions (fetch_record_{seed}_N and similar) raise it for any id below 1, before doing any work. (3) Never return None or an error dict to signal bad input. (4) Batch functions don't raise; they follow the partial-result contract. (5) The offending id may appear in the exception message but never in logs; the logging rule still applies. (6) Tests cover id 0 and a negative id. Alternatives: returning Optional (rejected: ambiguous with not-found) and a Result type (rejected: unidiomatic in this codebase). (7) Rollout - the first fetcher to validate its input introduces the class; the rest adopt it as they are touched, rather than in one sweeping change, to keep diffs reviewable. (8) Callers that currently check for None after a fetch keep working until their fetcher is migrated, then switch to catching RecordInputError.

variants.title: Never log record ids or function arguments
variants.content: Never log record ids or function arguments from the record service, because compliance treats request data as customer data; log counts and durations instead.

variants.title: Never log record ids or function arguments
variants.content: Never log record ids or function arguments in app/svc_{seed}_core.py, because compliance classifies request data as customer data and the log pipeline isn't approved for it (audit finding, June 2026). That includes debug logs and messages passed to logger.exception; log counts and durations instead. If an error needs an id to be debuggable, put it in the exception for the caller to handle, not in a log line. The audit sampled two weeks of logs and found ids in debug output from three modules; this one was cleaned up first. Applies to print() as well, since stdout is shipped to the same pipeline.

variants.title: Keep request data out of the record service's logs
variants.content: Keep request data out of the record service's logs, because the June 2026 audit classified record ids as customer data. Plan: (1) Never log record ids, function arguments or returned records, at any level, including debug. (2) Log what operators need without request data: that a call happened, counts and durations. (3) Exceptions may carry an id for the caller, but logger.exception messages must not include it. (4) print() follows the same rule, since stdout ships to the same pipeline. (5) Use the module logger, logging.getLogger(__name__), so levels can be set per module.

seed_decisions.title: Return a tombstone for deleted records
seed_decisions.content: Return a tombstone, {'id': record_id, 'deleted': True}, for deleted records instead of raising, because the export job counts tombstones to reconcile deletions.

seed_decisions.title: Name hand-written functions verb_noun without the slot suffix
